notes:
I've put the notes together below. Five gaps first, so you know what's missing:
- **Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org):** I found nothing on this chapter.
- **Orthodox (oca.org) and newadvent.org:** I found nothing.
- **Wesley's own Notes:** the page wouldn't load. The Methodist material is one devotional from Seedbed, a Wesleyan publisher.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on this passage.
- **Modern scholarship:** I only saw NET Bible notes as they're quoted on preceptaustin.org. I didn't read bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org directly.

Where the traditions really differ is vv. 11–20: did Moses change God's mind?

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Israel wept over the report that Canaan's peoples were strong. In their unbelief they treated God's good gift of the land as if it were a bad thing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- He also notes the spies stood for the twelve tribes, so the spies' unbelief reflected the unbelief of most of Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Gill says "all the congregation" means mainly the leaders and elders who heard the report, though the news may have spread quickly into a general outcry. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/14-1.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary pictures the spies passing the news to their tribes, exaggerated as it spread through the camp, until everyone was weeping. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the grumbling was aimed at Moses and Aaron, but they were God's appointed leaders, so it was really grumbling against God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Pulpit thinks the people probably suspected Moses and Aaron of acting for their own gain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Preceptaustin notes that God later grants this very wish to die in the wilderness (vv. 28–29). The NET note it quotes adds that if they had wanted to die in Egypt, they shouldn't have cried to God to rescue them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- The Catholic Haydock commentary also says they got what they said they wanted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html

**v. 3**
- Matthew Henry calls it a blasphemous charge: as if God had brought them there on purpose to see them killed and their families taken. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_014.cfm
- Haydock likewise says that in their anger they credit God with an evil plan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html
- Pulpit says the Hebrew is better read "why *is* the Lord bringing us," since they were only at the edge of the land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Preceptaustin points out that their wives would die in the wilderness, but God says their children would not (vv. 31–33). https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary

**v. 4**
- Pulpit calls this a new height of rebellion. Before, they had only wished to be back in Egypt; now they proposed actually doing it. Choosing their own captain meant rejecting the "Captain of the Lord's host." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Guzik: "said to one another" shows they trusted a majority vote over God, and wanted a leader who would represent their rebellion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Haydock (Catholic) mentions older views that they wanted a king, or even another god. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html

**v. 5**
- The NET note (via preceptaustin) says falling facedown shows humility before God, not before the people. It is a posture of intercessory prayer, and here it holds off God's immediate anger. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- Guzik says they prayed without a word to the people, knowing only a miracle would save Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/

**v. 6**
- Guzik: tearing their clothes was a sign of mourning, as if someone had died or was about to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Haydock says it showed disapproval and zeal, meant to make the people stop and think. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html

**v. 7**
- Guzik: they had seen with their own eyes that God's promise of a good land was true, so they could trust his promise that they would win it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/

**v. 8**
- Pulpit notes Moses uses the same phrase, "the LORD delights in," in Deuteronomy 10:15. The only doubt in the whole matter was the doubt carried by that "if." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- A writer quoted on preceptaustin says the "if" was not really in question: God plainly did delight in them, since he had freed them, provided for them and promised them the land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary

**v. 9**
- "Bread for us," says Pulpit, means "we shall easily devour them." It may also mean the enemy would end up feeding Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Wiersbe (via preceptaustin) notes the reversal: the ten spies said the land would eat Israel up; Joshua and Caleb said Israel would eat up the Canaanites. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- Haydock says the Hebrew for "protection" is literally "their shadow." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html
- Henry: with God present they had nothing to fear, and their only real danger was turning God into their enemy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_014.cfm
- Guzik: their fear was willful rebellion, so Joshua and Caleb appealed to the people's will to turn back to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/

**v. 10**
- The Pulpit Homiletics notes that stoning was God's appointed penalty for serious crimes. The people turned it on Joshua and Caleb, treating them as the lawbreakers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/14.htm
- Preceptaustin links this to Exodus 17:4, where Moses feared being stoned. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- Ellicott thinks the glory appeared in the tabernacle court or above it, because the people could not have seen it inside. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-14.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik: God had only ever been good to Israel, so rejecting him made no sense and his "how long?" was fair. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Preceptaustin links this "contempt" or "spurning" with v. 23 and with Korah in Numbers 16:30. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- Haydock quotes Origen: God cannot be angry; he only foretells what will happen. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html

**v. 12**
- Guzik takes the offer as real: if Moses had done nothing, God would have built a new Israel from Moses. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Pulpit disagrees. Choosing Moses would have kept God's promise to Abraham, but the offer was neither a settled plan nor a flash of temper, since God never meant to cast off Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Preceptaustin notes this was the second such offer, after the golden calf. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary

**vv. 13–16**
- Pulpit says the broken Hebrew grammar of v. 13 suggests Moses' own words, jumbled by strong emotion. He never thought of himself or took up the offer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Haydock gives the same explanation for the unfinished sentence. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html
- Guzik: Moses appeals to God's reputation among the nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- On v. 16, Pulpit says pagan nations couldn't grasp that moral reasons might hold God back. They would only conclude he lacked the power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Preceptaustin compares Exodus 32:12. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- Haydock adds that God swore to give the land to the Hebrews, not to this particular generation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html

**v. 17**
- Preceptaustin: God's power would show by bringing Israel into a land held by giants. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- Henry: saving such a weak and unworthy people despite everything would make God's power look greatest. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Num/Num_014.cfm

**v. 18**
- Preceptaustin: Moses quotes Exodus 34:6–7, which he had seen proved true after the golden calf. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- Pulpit: Moses reminds God that forgiving is the most God-like of his rights. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Haydock: Moses names even the warning about punishment, knowing God's qualities never conflict. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html
- Poole (on biblehub) offers another rendering: "in destroying he will not utterly destroy." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/14-18.htm

**v. 19**
- Preceptaustin: Moses rests his plea on God's great mercy, not on how hard he pleads. Wiersbe adds that God's past forgiveness is a further reason Moses gives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- TGC: Moses doesn't expect the people to improve. In effect he asks God to keep his word. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/article/did-moses-change-gods-mind/

**v. 20**
- Pulpit: the pardon is announced at once and without conditions, even though limits follow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Ellicott: God's justice still required punishment, but the people were not wiped out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-14.html
- Gill: the pardon means they would not all be killed at once, and it shows the power of a righteous man's prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/14-20.htm
- Haydock (Catholic): the sin is forgiven but its punishment must still be served, just later than threatened. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html

**v. 21**
- Pulpit translates it "as I live, and the glory of the Lord shall fill all the earth": a second clause paired with the first. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Haydock: the whole world will see it was Israel's sin, not God's weakness, that kept them out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html

**v. 22**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew word here doesn't mean "because." It begins the content of God's oath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- On "ten times," Ellicott mentions attempts to list ten actual rebellions, but thinks ten more likely means "a full measure." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/
- Haydock (Catholic) agrees it means "very often." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html
- Pulpit thinks the Levites and Joshua were probably not included in this sentence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm

---

**Where the traditions differ: did Moses change God's mind? (vv. 11–20)**
- **Reformed (Sproul, Ligonier):** God knows everything and doesn't change, so Moses didn't change his mind. God plans both the outcome and the means. His threat carried an unspoken condition: if someone pleaded for the people, he would show grace. Prayer mostly changes us. https://learn.ligonier.org/qas/numbers-14-it-appears-moses-changed-mind-god-how-c
- **Reformed (Gospel Coalition):** The wilderness was a test, so vv. 11–12 were a test of Moses' faith, not a change of plan. Moses is a picture of Christ, the greater mediator. https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/article/did-moses-change-gods-mind/
- **Guzik (Calvary Chapel; listed under charismatic on your list):** "According to your word" means the prayer really mattered. It isn't a game where God makes a threat he never means. We should pray as if life and death hang on it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
  - But in his notes on Exodus 32 he says the language is written from a human point of view. Prayer changed the people's standing before God, not God himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-32/
- **Wesleyan (J.D. Walt, Seedbed):** He doesn't take up the question. He stresses Moses' Christ-like love for difficult people, rooted in remembering that God never gave up on him. (A reader comment below the post calls it a test, but that is not the author's view.) https://seedbed.com/beoad-the-love-of-god-and-the-love-of-moses-2/
- **Baptist (Spurgeon, via preceptaustin):** Moses "stood in the breach" and turned God's anger aside, as a picture of Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-14-commentary
- **Open theism (described by Don Stewart, who rejects it):** God really did change his mind. The traditional reading, Stewart reports, would make Moses' prayer meaningless. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/stewart_don/faq/does-god-know-everything/24-did-moses-persuade-god-to-change-his-mind.cfm

**Catholic reading (Haydock, 1859)**
- On v. 24, Haydock adds that Caleb was faithful by God's free grace, yet his cooperation earned a reward (citing Augustine). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html
- On v. 34, it reports that Jerome hoped many of this generation were saved in the end, because they had time to repent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/numbers-14.html
